data.title: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1
data.excerpt: Nika, a member of our association, joined the international crew of Danuvina Alacris — an exact copy of a 4th-century Roman lusoria patrol boat — for the Hungarian stage of its voyage down the Danube. She wrote this report exclusively for our site: on how the ship was built, on the Roman province of Pannonia and on the first stop at Aquincum.

children.text: In August, Nika, a member of our association, took part in an exceptional and wonderful event – she sailed down the Danube on an exact copy of a Roman ship. She wrote a report from this voyage exclusively for our site, which I am delighted to publish here.
ROMA AETERNA · ROMA INVICTA · DANUVINA ALACRIS!

The ship Danuvina Alacris, built using only Roman technological methods and period materials, is sailing down the Danube from Ingolstadt in Germany all the way to Romania as the culmination of the international Living Danube Limes project, which runs from 15 July 2022 to 4 November 2022. During this period it will cover a distance of 2,400 kilometres along the Danube from Germany to the Black Sea. From 2023 it will be exhibited at each pilot site for one year. In Slovakia we had the chance to see it a few weeks ago; it has sailed through Hungary and is currently in Croatia.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: I took up the unique opportunity of being a member of the international crew during the 4th stage of the voyage in neighbouring Hungary. Every day people had the chance to look at the ship close up, learn its story and glimpse the life of the Romans on the frontier of the Roman Empire. The voyage began in Germany in July and will end on 19 October 2022 in Romania. “Danuvina Alacris”, which is a replica of a lusoria-type ship of the 4th century AD, covers an average of 40 km a day, all of it under oars. The crew consists of up to 24 rowers and two helmsmen. The participants come from all over the world, so the language on board is English. From my own experience, however, I can say that a peculiar dialect containing words from various countries developed on board very quickly. Each section of the Danube is planned to take two weeks. The voyage is accompanied by festivals of just about every genre. Everywhere we were welcomed by enthusiastic locals, delighted at the arrival of a rare visitor on a unique vessel.

Overnight stays are sometimes in hotels, but mostly in school buildings, in halls of various facilities or in tents at campsites. During the 4th stage we slept in tents almost all the time, which proved only one thing. Stepping out of your comfort zone and pushing your limits is a test that gives far more than it takes.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: The purpose of the project is to connect the communities along the Danube and along the “limes”, a frontier that stretches across time, space, nationalities and sometimes also historical differences.

The whole project shows how the Danube, the limes and the ship connect us here in Central Europe. But the voyage also proved that something far stronger connects us: the enthusiasm of the local inhabitants, of the rowers and the crew members from various countries, of the organisers and of the local authorities. It is thanks to all these people that this voyage became an unforgettable experience. Together we all shared the excitement of the voyage and tried to keep a single rhythm, enduring high temperatures and the glare of the sun. Amusing situations as well as physically demanding moments made us friends regardless of sex, age, nationality or education.

The crew of the 4th stage was made up of various nationalities. There were three of us from Slovakia, one Catalan, a young man from Lithuania, a father and son from Hungary, two ever-smiling female students from the United Kingdom and a group from Germany and Austria. The youngest member was Andráš, only 13 years old, who managed the whole thing; for his effort we all rewarded him with a diploma reading JIUVENIS ROMANUS NAVIGATOR.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: The ship

Prof. Dr Boris Dreyer supervised the construction of the Danuvina Alacris as project manager for the project partner Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU). In his research he focuses on the history of Athenian democracy, Greek and Roman historiography and the history of the period from the end of the Republic to the middle imperial period. His research interests are connected with the editing of literary and epigraphic texts. A further focus of his work lies in the popularisation of scholarship, for example in connection with the reconstruction of ancient ships. Before the launch of the Living Danube Limes project he was responsible for building the imperial patrol boat Friedericiana Alexandrina Navis (F.A.N.), which set out on its first voyage in 2018.

Prof. Dr Boris Dreyer supervised the construction of the Danuvina Alacris as project manager for the project partner Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU). In his research he focuses on the history of Athenian democracy, Greek and Roman historiography and the history of the period from the end of the Republic to the middle imperial period. His research interests are connected with the editing of literary and epigraphic texts. A further focus of his work lies in the popularisation of scholarship, for example in connection with the reconstruction of ancient ships. Before the launch of the Living Danube Limes project he was responsible for building the imperial patrol boat Friedericiana Alexandrina Navis (F.A.N.), which set out on its first voyage in 2018.

In the German city of Mainz there is a museum of Roman ships with several ship fragments and other finds, plus a number of excellent reconstructions, which have been the basis of ideas and research on shipbuilding and on how ships and rowers functioned in the ancient world. On the basis of the remains of the Roman shipwrecks discovered in Mainz, the University reconstructed a late Roman Danube ship of the 4th century AD. 
Danuvina Alacris belongs to a type of patrol boat commonly used in late antiquity. The ship is 18 metres long and its draught is about 40 cm. Spruce oars belong to the ship. 49 pieces were made with a length of 4.10 m and 4 pieces with a length of 4.70 or 4.40 m. Its hull is built from 18 oak trunks, some of which are 20 metres long. The oaks were felled in the week from 9 to 14 November 2020.
Danuvina Alacris was built for an assumed number of 20 rowers. The shape and the material (spruce) of the oars needed could be determined with certainty, but their length was unclear and was therefore the subject of several experiments. For this reason they were made in two different lengths: 4.1 m and 4.7 m. The oak steering oar consists of two parts lashed together. They were planed by the Roman method, which was faithfully reproduced from the finds. Planing is hard work, because you have to make sure the oars are uniform. It is also possible that knots will become visible after planing the squared timber. These then represent a predetermined breaking point.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text:
Roman nails (about 4,000 were made, about 3,500 were used in building the ship) and shield bosses were forged with the help of a Roman forge. The use of metal items in the construction was minimal; wooden pegs were also used as joints to connect the individual parts. The floorboards and other parts of the ship were treated with linseed oil.
The exterior coating is hot wax mixed with colourant by encaustic, that is, a partly saponified variant of beeswax, which was tested with various pigments. The white substance is an adaptation of the recipe for “Punic wax” according to Pliny and can be used as a binding base. The new recipe has now been applied to the oak planks of the starboard and port sides in the zone above the water line. Danuvina Alacris has a stork and eyes on her shield. The stork motif was chosen on the basis of the motif on the standard of the 3rd Roman legion - Vexillum of Legio III Italica.
Why does Danuvina Alacris have eyes?

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text:
This custom comes from the shipbuilders of Greece. The ancient Greeks believed that a ship was alive with them, and so it had eyes painted above the bow so that it could “see far ahead”.
The ship's pump was found in the wreck of a merchant ship. It works by a lift-and-lower method (like a bicycle pump). The pump for the ship Danuvina Alacris is made of bronze and is thus demonstrably connected with shipping. This pump is highly efficient, with an output of up to about 16 litres per minute.
Shields are also part of the ship's basic equipment. The motif used to decorate the shields was the Victoria from the finds in the collections at Dura Europos. It depicts a winged woman holding a palm branch in her hands and standing on a globe. The shields for the ship Danuvina Alacris were made of poplar wood.
For painting the Victoria motif, colours determined experimentally in advance were used, with only naturally occurring pigments. The Victoria motif is not attested on shields of this kind, but it could belong to the period around AD 260. The shields are secured at the rim with cowhide and at the front with a shield boss.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text:
Thanks to the Roman strategy of protecting the frontiers of their empire, forts and towns were built in a regular scheme in the Danube basin. They are often described as a cultural treasure and many of them are protected today and inscribed on the UNESCO List of World Natural and Cultural Heritage. Thanks to the international Living Danube Limes project, important Roman monuments on the Danube have been investigated by the most modern geophysical methods (for example the Matrica camp, which we will deal with in the next part). Through them scholars have gained valuable new insights and have filled research gaps concerning the “Danube limes”.
A vessel of the Lusoria type, among which we also count "our" ship, was approximately 17 to 21 metres long, with a maximum width of 2.5 metres and a height of about 90 cm. Given the limited space, the crew of the ship were the soldiers themselves. There could be 27 to 35 men, 24 to 32 of them rowers, with 2 men serving the ship and the sail and one helmsman, who was probably also the ship's commander.

children.text: The province of Pannonia

Pannonia (Lat. Pannonia) was a Roman province between the middle Danube and the Sava, established under the emperor Augustus in the years 6–9 after the so-called Pannonian revolt (the territory of the future province had already been conquered in 12–9 BC). It extended over what is today western Hungary (Transdanubia), eastern Austria (chiefly the Vienna Basin), Slovakia (only Petržalka, Jarovce, Rusovce, Čunovo and the possible forelands of the Limes Romanus along the Danube), part of Slovenia, northern Croatia and Serbia in the region of Sirmium. The name Pannonia was used for centuries after the demise of Roman military and civil power in this region (around the year 400).
It was originally inhabited by Illyrians and Celts, who were Romanised at the end of the 1st century BC. The founding of new settlements and the building of forts, especially along the Limes Romanus, contributed to this. Pannonia was originally joined administratively with Dalmatia in the province of Illyria, and in the year 9 it became independent. Under Trajan it was divided into Upper Pannonia (Pannonia Superior; the western part) with its capital at Carnuntum and Lower Pannonia (Pannonia Inferior; the eastern part) with its capital at Aquincum (today's Óbuda district). Under Diocletian a reorganisation took place: from Pannonia Superior arose Pannonia Prima in the north and Pannonia Savia in the south, and from Pannonia Inferior, Pannonia Valeria in the north and Pannonia Secunda in the south.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: All the attacks of the Germanic tribes from the territory of present-day Slovakia were directed into Pannonia and, conversely, the Romans penetrated from Pannonia into the territory of present-day Slovakia. Military, trade and cultural contacts between the inhabitants of the territory of present-day Slovakia and the Roman Empire were conducted through Pannonia. At the end of the 4th and the beginning of the 5th century the Germanic tribes of the Vandals and the Goths seized Pannonia. In 433 Rome officially ceded the territory to the Huns. In the second quarter of the 5th century, especially under Attila, it belonged to the central areas of the Hunnic Empire. After its collapse it was controlled by the Gepids and the Langobards.

At the end of the 5th and the beginning of the 6th century the Slavs began to penetrate especially into northern Pannonia. In the middle of the 6th century the Avars settled in Pannonia and created an extensive empire, which was destroyed by the armies of Charlemagne at the turn of the 8th and 9th centuries. After the decline of Avar power the Slavs also settled southern Pannonia. In the second half of the 9th century the Balaton Principality arose here, and for a few years the northern part belonged to Great Moravia. In the 9th century only the surroundings of Carnuntum (between Tulln, Győr and Szombathely) were designated Upper Pannonia, and the remaining territory Lower Pannonia.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: The way in which the Romans managed to rule their vast empire with the help of a relatively small mercenary army was highly effective and fairly stable, even though they too did not escape a number of revolts.

The Romans were not only experts in the application of force and violence; they also had an extraordinary talent for winning the support of the peoples they had subdued: they respected local traditions and ethnic particularities as long as these did not threaten their supremacy. They encouraged self-government and used only a relatively small imperial administration to hold the empire together. Members of the aristocracy moved across the empire from one office to another, and through the army even the most remote corner of the land came into contact with Rome. The army was, moreover, a catalyst that made possible the emergence of a new society on the frontier. The frontier was formed by fortified points, and an important function was the control of movement within the empire and out of it. This task was performed chiefly by scouts and by the river fleets, which controlled the land, the frontier rivers and the seas. The frontier was also a membrane through which the wealth of Roman ideas, as well as objects of everyday use, penetrated into the world on the other side of the border. Trade links which reached as far as India and further east, in the south to the Sahara and in the north to the Baltic Sea, brought the empire an enormous variety of goods and demonstrably influenced even lands that the Romans never occupied.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: The frontiers of the Roman Empire are part of the shared cultural heritage not only of the countries of the Mediterranean region. They were formed by a system of legionary camps, camps of auxiliary units and watchtowers, which made it possible to control the continuous territory of the Roman Empire. The individual points of the defensive system were linked by frontier roads. In expanding their empire in Europe the Romans halted at the Rhine and the Danube, which they used as natural frontiers. On the middle course of the Danube the province of Pannonia arose, with the legionary camps of Vindobona (Vienna, Austria), Carnuntum (Petronell, Austria), Brigetio (Komárom, Hungary) and Aquincum (Budapest, Hungary). Today the course of these frontiers is documented mainly by archaeological finds of walls, ditches, forts (castella), watchtowers and civilian settlements.
The voyage

During the voyage through Hungary we got to know the towns on the Danube in 14 days; we visited Aquincum in Budapest, the Matrica camp in Százhalombatta, Lusonnium in the town of DUNAKÖMLŐD, and we toured the museums in Baja, Dunaföldvár, Ercsi and many others. For history enthusiasts this region is rich, and not only in Roman monuments. Bronze Age sites are also of interest (for example the Bell Beaker culture, the Vatya culture, the burial mounds in the archaeological park and others) A special experience was the visit to the only nuclear power station, in the town of Paks (the largest producer of electricity in Hungary), which we toured in period dress, in tunics. This combination of history and modern energy generation was an experience not only for us but also for the employees of the power station.

children.text: Aquincum

The first important ancient stop where our ship dropped anchor was Aquincum, an ancient city lying on the north-eastern frontier of the province of Pannonia within the Roman Empire. Today the ruins of the city are to be found in Budapest, the capital of Hungary.

This site was originally settled by the Celtic tribe of the Eravisci. Aquincum served as a military base (castrum) and was part of the Roman frontier protection system known as the limes. Around AD 41–54 a 500-strong cavalry unit arrived, and by AD 89 a Roman legion of 6,000 men (Legio II Adiutrix) was stationed here. The town gradually grew up around the fort; Aquincum became the capital of the Roman province of Pannonia Inferior, a position it held until Diocletian's administrative reform more than a hundred years later. Under Hadrian the town acquired municipal status, while under Septimius Severus Aquincum became a colonia. As a centre of operations on the Roman frontier against the neighbouring Iazyges, Aquincum was occasionally the residence of emperors.

blocks.alt: Sailing the Danube in a Roman ship – part 1

children.text: At the end of the 2nd century the city had at least 30,000 inhabitants and covered a substantial part of the area known today as the Óbuda district of Budapest. The ruins of the old Roman occupation can also be seen in other parts of Budapest, especially in the town of Contra-Aquincum. During the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD these Roman buildings were the heart of the commercial life of the province of Pannonia. The excavations testify to the lifestyle of this period. From the beginning of the 3rd century Christianity began to spread in the city. During the middle of the 4th century the territory of Aquincum was under constant attack from the Sarmatians from the north. The decline of the Roman Empire affected Aquincum too, and the ancient city was largely destroyed by AD 350. Germanic peoples and the Huns invaded the region during AD 409. The people living in the settlement were able to enjoy the achievements of the empire, such as central heating in the houses, public baths, a mithraeum and palaces. The most important monuments in Aquincum are the two amphitheatres: the Civil Amphitheatre of Aquincum and the Military Amphitheatre of Aquincum, built in the 1st century AD. They were venues for gladiatorial contests and fights with animals. Many historical artefacts from the city are now in the Aquincum Museum. A reconstruction of the hydraulic system is displayed in the museum. Roman houses and paintings that were found at the site. In the vicinity of the city the ruins of a three-storey aqueduct were discovered, many of which can still be seen today.
